title: Shahid Kapoor Has Stopped Trusting His Own Instincts. That Might Be the Smartest Thing He's Ever Done.
excerpt: In a searingly honest THR India cover story, the actor admits his pursuit of art-meets-commerce tore him apart — and reveals why Cocktail 2 marks a deliberate new chapter
body:
There's a photograph on the June cover of *The Hollywood Reporter India* that tells you everything before you read a single word. **Shahid Kapoor** looks directly into the camera — not performing, not smouldering, not doing the intense-dark-hero thing that has defined his last half-dozen roles. He just looks settled. A little tired, maybe. Honest. It's the face of a man who has stopped pretending he has it all figured out.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=JBOkML4Ld9g</youtube>

In a sweeping conversation with **Anupama Chopra**, the actor opens up with a candour that Bollywood cover stories rarely permit. And the headline revelation is startling: after 23 years in the industry, Shahid Kapoor no longer trusts his own instincts when choosing a film.

> "I might be driven by a very pure artistic instinct, and that might not always land for me. I now insist on doing narrations not alone. I used to always do them alone." — Shahid Kapoor

That admission carries weight when you consider the trajectory. *Deva* underperformed. *O'Romeo*, despite being one of his most committed performances, failed to connect at the box office. These weren't lazy films — they were bold, personal choices that Shahid made because they spoke to him as an artist. The problem, he now concedes, is that what speaks to an artist doesn't always speak to an audience.

"What hurts me the most is when they walk out of the theater unsatisfied," he says. "I have failed at some level if the film didn't land because maybe I didn't make the right choice."

## The art-commerce split

The most revealing moment in the interview comes when Shahid articulates a tension that has quietly shaped his entire career. He spent years trying to fuse the intensity of his *Haider* and *Kaminey* instincts with the commercial scale that Hindi cinema demands. It didn't work.

"I spent most of my career trying to bring two things together which I don't think naturally sit together," he says, before adding with disarming finality: "I've told myself to stop trying to bring these two things together, because it's tearing you apart."

Coming from a man who has swung between *Jab We Met* and *Udta Punjab*, between a mainstream blockbuster and a National Film Award, this isn't defeat — it's clarity. And it helps explain why his next move is **Cocktail 2**, a romantic entertainer directed by **Homi Adajania**, co-starring **Kriti Sanon** and **Rashmika Mandanna**, releasing June 19.

"After very long I'm playing a character that's not alpha, hard, or grey and edgy," Shahid says of his role as Kunal. "I'm playing an extremely likeable, warm and endearing character."

For fans who fell in love with him in *Ishq Vishk* and *Vivah*, this is the return they didn't know they were waiting for. For Shahid, it's a deliberate surrender — not to the audience's nostalgia, but to the idea that a film can be emotionally genuine without needing to prove how serious it is.

## The industry's script crisis

Shahid doesn't stop at self-reflection. When the conversation turns to the well-documented shortage of strong original scripts in Hindi cinema, he identifies a root cause others have danced around: the industry drove its writers away.

"We went through a phase where we were only making remakes and franchise movies," he says, "and I'm sure there were writers sitting out there with good content who got tired and just left."

It's the kind of observation that sounds obvious after someone says it. But it takes a certain confidence — or perhaps a certain exhaustion with pretence — to say it on a magazine cover. He goes further, pointing to social media as a corrosive force: the manufactured trends, the inorganic perception-building, the economics of visibility that reward noise over craft.

## What's next?

After **Cocktail 2** and **Farzi 2** (which begins filming later this year), Shahid says he has nothing lined up. "I don't know what I'm going to do after that," he admits — and there's no anxiety in it. After two decades of chasing, calculating, second-guessing, and rebuilding, doing nothing might be the most intentional choice he's made.

For NRI audiences who grew up on his *Ishq Vishk* charm and later watched him transform into one of Hindi cinema's most versatile actors, this interview lands differently. It's not a press junket. It's a reckoning. And **Cocktail 2** — a glossy, three-way love story backed by **Maddock Films** and **Luv Films**, already the most anticipated Indian film on IMDb — feels less like a career bet and more like a man who finally stopped overthinking and chose to have fun.

*Cocktail 2 releases in theatres on June 19.*
